property_summary: For any initialize(...) call, the reference implementation always stores the passed _baseToken in C.baseToken; the mutant that unconditionally sets baseToken to address(0) will cause baseToken() != _baseToken for some fuzzed _baseToken values (e.g. any non-zero address).

For any caller and any _baseToken parameter, a correct pool sets baseToken to the provided _baseToken when initialize(...) returns successfully; the mutant incorrectly sets baseToken to msg.sender for some inputs (when msg.sender != _baseToken), breaking this property.

For any inputs to initialize, the contract's public baseToken getter must equal the _baseToken argument passed (reference preserves baseToken == _baseToken); the mutant that assigns baseToken = _nft breaks this by making baseToken != _baseToken for some inputs.

For any inputs to initialize(...), the reference contract sets the public baseToken state variable to the _baseToken argument (so c.baseToken() == _baseToken after initialize returns); the mutant that deletes that assignment can leave baseToken unchanged, violating this property for some inputs.

For any inputs to initialize(...), the reference contract sets baseToken to the provided _baseToken; the mutant overwrites baseToken to address(this), so there exist inputs where c.baseToken() != the provided _baseToken (i.e. the stored baseToken differs from the initializer argument).

For any inputs to initialize, the deployed contract's nft public getter returns the _nft address passed into initialize; the mutant that sets nft = address(0) breaks this by making nft() == address(0) for some (indeed many) inputs.

After initialize(_baseToken,_nft,...) completes successfully, the contract's nft() equals the _nft argument; the mutant assigns nft = _baseToken so for some fuzzed inputs nft() != _nft and the property is violated.
For any caller and any _nft argument, after initialize(...) completes the contract's nft() should equal the provided _nft; the mutant that assigns nft = msg.sender breaks this when caller != _nft.
After initialize(...) returns, nft() equals the _nft argument for any caller; the mutant that sets nft = msg.sender breaks this whenever caller != _nft.

For any initialize(...) call the contract's stored changeFee equals the provided _changeFee (i.e. changeFee == _changeFee); the mutant doubles the stored value so for some fuzzed _changeFee the equality fails.

For any inputs to initialize, the reference contract stores the provided _changeFee into changeFee; the mutant overwrites it to zero for some nonzero _changeFee, so changeFee == _changeFee holds for all inputs in the reference but can be false for the mutant.

For any initialize(...) call, the contract's stored changeFee equals the _changeFee argument supplied (i.e., changeFee == _changeFee); the mutant adds one to the stored value so for some fuzzed _changeFee inputs the stored changeFee != _changeFee and the property is violated.

For any inputs to initialize(...) the reference contract reverts if _feeRate > 5000 so initialization only succeeds when c.feeRate() == _feeRate with _feeRate <= 5000; the mutant removes that check allowing initialization with feeRate > 5000, so there exist inputs where the mutant accepts a _feeRate > 5000 while the reference would have reverted (i.e., reference never results in c.feeRate() > 5000 but mutant can).

For any feeRate input the correct contract accepts (does not revert) initialize when _feeRate <= 5000 and sets feeRate to that value; the mutant incorrectly reverts for those inputs (it only accepts >5000), so there exists inputs (e.g. any _feeRate <= 5000) where P allows initialization but M rejects it.

For any input to initialize, the correct contract sets feeRate equal to the supplied _feeRate; the mutant sets feeRate to 0 regardless, so there exists inputs where c.feeRate() != _feeRate (mutant breaks this).

For any inputs, calling initialize on a freshly-deployed C should succeed exactly once and future calls must revert due to AlreadyInitialized; the mutant that removes the revert allows a second initialize call to succeed, violating that one-time-initialization property.

For any inputs, the original contract allows initialize(...) to succeed when the pool is not yet initialized (initialized transitions from false to true); the mutant inverts the check and therefore initialize(...) must revert when initialized is false, breaking that property for some inputs.
